args.text:
Now, ya might've heard this one. I reckon, hand on heart, the good Lord who made the lot of us made everything in New England bar the weather. Who makes that? Dunno. But my money's on a mob of raw apprentices out the back of the weather-clerk's factory, learning the ropes in New England for board and clothes. Once they've got the hang of it they get bumped up to making weather for the countries that want a decent article, the ones that'll take their custom down the road if they don't get it. Because there's a lavish variety to New England weather, I tell ya. A stranger looks at it and admires it—and then regrets it. The weather over there's never knocking off. Always at work, always minding the shop, always cooking up some new design and trying it on the locals to see how it goes. And spring's its busiest season by a mile. One spring I counted a hundred and thirty-six different kinds of weather inside twenty-four hours. A hundred and thirty-six! Not a word of a lie.

Now, it was me that made the name and fortune of that bloke with the marvellous collection of weather on show at the Centennial, the one that knocked the foreigners for six. He was all set to go round the world collecting specimens from every clime there is. I grabbed him and I said, "Don't you do it, mate. You come to New England on a good spring day." And I gave him the full rundown on what we could turn out for style, variety and quantity. So he came. Made his whole collection in four days. Four days! Variety? He owned up he'd got hundreds of kinds of weather he'd never even heard of. Quantity? Well, once he'd picked out and chucked every bit with the slightest blemish on it, he still had weather enough, and weather to spare. Weather to hire out, weather to sell, weather to stick in the bank, weather to invest, weather to give to the poor. Weather coming out his ears, basically.

Mind you, New Englanders are patient, easygoing types by nature, but there's some things they just won't put up with. Every year they do in a fair few poets for writing about "Beautiful Spring." Mostly they're blow-ins, see, who've brought their idea of spring from somewhere else, and of course they've got no way of knowing how the locals feel about spring. So the first thing they know, the chance to ask how the locals feel has gone for good. Should've asked earlier, ay.

Then there's Old Probabilities, the forecaster. Mighty reputation for getting it right, and fair enough, he's earned every bit of it. You pick up the paper and watch him tick 'em off, crisp and confident as you like: here's today's weather on the Pacific, down South, in the Middle States, round Wisconsin. Sailing along, proud as punch with his powers, till he hits New England. And then watch his tail drop. He's got no idea. Not a clue what New England's going to do. So he scratches his noggin over it for a bit, and eventually he comes out with something like this: Probably northeast to southwest winds, varying to the southward and westward and eastward, and points between, high and low barometer swapping around from place to place; probable areas of rain, snow, hail, and drought, succeeded or preceded by earthquakes, with thunder and lightning. Covers the lot, doesn't it? But then, with his mind off wandering, he jots a postscript on the bottom to cover accidents: "But it is possible that the programme may be wholly changed in the mean time." Hedging his bets, the poor bugger.

Yep, one of the shiniest gems in New England's weather is how dazzlingly uncertain it is. There's only one thing you can be sure of: there'll be heaps of it—a proper grand parade. You just can never tell which end of the procession's going to move off first. You get yourself set for the drought, leave your brolly at home and head out, and it's two to one you come back drowned. You make up your mind the earthquake's due, so you stand clear, grab hold of something to steady yourself, and next thing you know—bang—you're struck by lightning. Big letdowns, those. But what can ya do?

And the lightning over there's a funny thing. It's that convincing that when it hits something, it doesn't leave enough of it behind for you to tell whether—well, you'd reckon it was something valuable and a pollie had been through. Cleaned the place out. And the thunder! When it's only tuning up, scraping and sawing and getting the instruments ready for the show, the strangers go, "Strewth, that's awful thunder you've got here!" But once the baton goes up and the real concert kicks off, where's your stranger? Down the cellar with his head in the ash-barrel, that's where.
